explanations.explanation: Solomon, Israel's king, says it straight: "Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain." The builders can haul and hammer all day, but without Him the work is in vain. I've pressed a lot of dough in my day, and I know the feeling of working hard on something that needed more than me. Solomon puts the LORD at the center of the whole building.

Good guess, since Solomon is a king himself and could have said, "Get my stamp on it." But he points higher than any throne. The psalm says "Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain." Even the king's own house depends on the LORD.

Speed never comes up in this verse, friend. I know bakers who treat the oven timer like a race, but Solomon isn't counting minutes. He says "Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain." It's about WHO builds, not how quick.

I get why this feels true, since watchmen are the ones staying up all night. But Solomon, Israel's king, says "unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain." The guarding isn't the thing that makes the city safe. The LORD protecting it is.

That's it. Solomon, Israel's king, says "unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain." The watchmen do their job, but it's the LORD who protects the city. Wide-open eyes can't do what He does.

"For He gives sleep to His beloved." That's the end of verse 2. Solomon, Israel's king, says rising early and staying up late, toiling for bread to eat, is in vain, and then he gives a gift: rest. A whole verse about working, and it lands on a pillow.

Gold sounds like a nice reward, but this verse isn't handing out treasure. Solomon, Israel's king, says "He gives sleep to His beloved." Sleep is what the psalm names as the gift. I'd take a good night's rest over a pile of gold coins any day, and I've got a lot of nights to make up for.

Land is a solid guess, but it's not in this verse. The line says "He gives sleep to His beloved." Solomon, Israel's king, is talking about rest after all that rising early and staying up late. No deed to the property, just a good night's sleep.
"Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD." That's how verse 3 begins. A heritage is something handed to you, and the psalm says the LORD is the One handing it.

It's easy to think you earn everything with sweat, and I know that feeling after a long day at the ovens. But the psalm doesn't say that here. It says "Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD." The source it names is Him.
The king is the one writing this psalm, so you'd think he'd take the credit. But Solomon, Israel's king, doesn't. He says "Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD." The credit goes to the LORD.
Yes! Verse 3 says "the fruit of the womb is His reward." A reward is something given, not something you grab. The psalm says it comes from the LORD.

It's actually true. Verse 3 says "the fruit of the womb is His reward." That means children are called the LORD's reward right in the text. The first half of the verse already named them a heritage from the LORD, and this line backs it up.

"Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them." That's verse 5, loud and clear. Solomon, Israel's king, has just compared children to arrows, so a full quiver is a good sight to him. The word he picks is blessed.

I can picture a man with a full quiver looking worn out, honestly, because full hands are a lot of work. But that's not the word in the psalm. It says "Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them." The man gets called blessed.
Envied is a fun word, but it's not the one in the verse. The psalm doesn't talk about what other people think of him. It says "Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them." The word is blessed.

explanations.answer: When he confronts enemies at the gate
explanations.explanation: The verse says "He will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate." That's the moment Solomon, Israel's king, names. The man with the full quiver is not put to shame there. A gate is a place where the city meets whoever comes.

explanations.answer: When he stands before the king
explanations.explanation: Standing before a king would make anybody's knees wobble, mine included. But the psalm doesn't mention a king here. It says the man "will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate." The setting is the gate.

explanations.answer: When he brings his offering to the priest
explanations.explanation: An offering is a good Bible image, but it's not in this verse. The psalm says he "will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate." No priest, no altar, just the gate.
"Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!" That's how this song opens. It's one big blessing before anything else gets said. The word "all" is right there in the text.

The first song talked about houses, so I get the mix-up. But this one opens a different way. It says "Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!" The blessing goes to those who fear the LORD.

explanations.answer: All who rise early to work
explanations.explanation: Early risers get a lot of credit in my bakery, and my oven timer agrees. But this song isn't giving the blessing to them. It says "Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!" The blessed ones fear the LORD.

Right on. The song says "Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!" The second half is how the song describes them: they walk in His ways. They're people who fear the LORD AND walk in His ways.

This one's actually true. The opening line says "Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!" Walking in His ways is part of how the song describes them. Easy to miss when the line goes by fast.
Verse 2 says "For when you eat the fruit of your labor, blessings and prosperity will be yours." It's a gift that comes with the work. The song names two things, and those are the two.
Those are two lovely things, but they're not what this verse says. It says "blessings and prosperity will be yours." That's the promise when you eat the fruit of your labor.
Honor and fame sound like a nice trophy, but the song doesn't say that. Verse 2 says "blessings and prosperity will be yours." It's blessings and prosperity, with no spotlight mentioned.

explanations.answer: It's full of life and growth
explanations.explanation: A vine that's fruitful and flourishing is a living, growing thing. I think that's the picture: a house with life in it. The song says "Your wife will be like a fruitful vine flourishing within your house."
Nothing in the verse says anything needs trimming. The song says "Your wife will be like a fruitful vine flourishing within your house." A flourishing vine is a good thing to see in a house.
A flourishing vine isn't sitting still, friend. It's growing and bearing fruit. The song says "Your wife will be like a fruitful vine flourishing within your house." That's a house with life in it.
The song says "your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table." Olive shoots are young, new growth, and here they're gathered at the table. It's a picture of a family together.

The gate showed up in the last song, so it's an easy one to grab. But this song keeps things inside the home. It says "your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table." The sons are at the table, not the gate.
Olive shoots do make you think of a field, and I understand the guess. But the song says "your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table." The sons are sitting at the table, indoors.
"In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who fears the LORD." That's verse 4, and it ties up what came before. The wife, the sons and the table all point to this word.
Trouble isn't what this song promises. Verse 4 says "In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who fears the LORD." The word is blessing, which matches how the song started.

Testing is a real part of life, and the Bible talks about it elsewhere. But this verse doesn't say it. It says "In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who fears the LORD." The word is blessing.

The song says "May the LORD bless you from Zion, that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life." It's a wish for the whole city's good, not only the family at the table. It lasts all the days of your life.
Babylon isn't in this song at all. The wish is "that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life." It's a hope for good things in Jerusalem, not for someone else's downfall.
Egypt never comes up in this song. The verse says "that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life." The sight in view is Jerusalem.
Yes, verse 6 says "that you may see your children’s children." That's the wish after Jerusalem's prosperity. The song then closes with "Peace be upon Israel!"
This one is true, friend. Verse 6 says "that you may see your children’s children." It's right there before the closing line, "Peace be upon Israel!"
